summary:
NASA has two major satellite fire records, which are MODIS and VIIRS. However, their results cannot be compared directly because VIIRS has sharp pixels and detects about five times more hotspots in Sabah. When both satellite records and combined together, the number of hotspots appears to double after 2012.
So, to reduce this difference, we developed a method to harmonise the two records and create a monthly record of fire hotspots in Sabah, Malaysia from 2003 to October 2026. We also built a web application that presents it in an interactive burning activity calendar. When tested on data for years that were not used to develop the method, we achieved a total error of about 24%, compared with around 80% without adjustment. The harmonised data also showed a 59% decrease in yearly hotspots counts instead of the apparent increase. 
Through our web application, land managers can explore seasonal fire patterns, identify years with the highest hotspot activity and compare the latest month’s activity with historical averages. However, values before 2012 are estimated, and satellite hotspots are detections rather than the actual area burned.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Borneo Burn Calendar is a web application that brings together 286 months of fire hotspots records in Sabah, from January 2003 to October 2026, into one consistent record.

- A status banner: Shows how the latest month’s fire activity compares with what is usual.

- ⁠A calendar matrix showing the hotspot activity for each month and year in four colour classes. Users can tap on a month to see more details. Estimated and provisional months are also marked.

- ⁠A toggle that lets users switch between the raw combined record and the harmonised record, so they are able to see the sudden jump in 2012 and how our method helps to correct it.

- Information on important burning periods and months with unusually high or low activity.⁠

- A “Now vs Normal” view that compares a selected month with the median hotspot count for the same month over the previous 10 years.

- Charts showing our results as proofs, a “How sure are we?” section, a list of limitations and an option to download the data as a CSV file.

HOW IT WORKS

1. We downloaded MODIS and VIIRS active fire activity records for Sabah from NASA FIRMS.

2. We cleaned both records using the same rules and counted the number of hotspots each month.

3. During the years when both satellites were operating, we found that VIIRS detected about 4.95 times more hotspots than MODIS in our study area.

4. ⁠To make the records more comparable, we multiplied the MODIS counts before February 2012 by this ratio. From February 2012 onwards, we used the actual VIIRS counts.

5. ⁠We then tested our method using data from years that were not used to develop it. We calculated the ratio using data from 2012–2018 and tested it on data from 2019–2025.


RESULTS

We tested the method on seven years it had never seen, 2019-2025.

- Without our method, the MODIS counts were inaccurate by about 80%.

- With our method, they were inaccurate by about 24%.

- The colour or level on the calendar was right in 72 of 84 months, 86%. It was never more than one colour or level off.

This means you can trust the calendar to show which months are busy, which are quiet, and when the season peaks. But you are not suggested to trust it for the exact number of hotspots in one single month before the year 2012.

HEADLINE FINDING

We compare two periods of years: 2003-2011 and 2012-2025.

- When joining the two satellite records as they are, the yearly hotspots seem to double (+100%). That jump is fake as it comes from the switching to a sharper sensor.

- After our method, yearly hotspots fell by about 59%.

Every check we ran shows a fall. The exact size is less certain than the direction.

HOW WE CHECKED OURSELVES

We tried to break our own method.

• We tried five other methods on the same test: a ratio for each calendar month (32% error), a power law (26%), a ratio for each region (24%), a straight line (23.5%), and a base plus ratio (22%). Our simple ratio scored 24%.

None was clearly better, and the best one failed in quiet months, so we kept the simple one.

• We ran four extra checks:

- The ratio stays between 4.2 and 6.1 every year, with no clear trend.

- Using both MODIS satellites (24% error) is better than Aqua alone (28%) or Terra alone (46%).

- Changing the confidence filters keeps the error at 24-25%.

- The fall in hotspots shows up in every check.

• Experiment B from the github repo tries to understand why the sensors differ. We matched Aqua and Suomi NPP passes from 2012 to 2022. Detections seen only by VIIRS are weaker (5.6 MW against 9.0 MW) and more often single pixels (54% against 25%). This is a pattern, not proof of the cause.

• One check proved us wrong. MODIS alone shows the same fall, but that is just the arithmetic. It does not prove our ratio. We corrected our wording.

WHO IT HELPS

Plantation and forestry managers who plan patrols, staffing, burn restrictions and fire services who plan for the season. It is a planning tool and not a live fire alert.

LIMITS

• Hotspots are satellite detections. They are not fires or burned area.

• Values before 2012 are estimates.

• Quiet months come out about 16% too low.

• The ratio is tested for Sabah only, and only with our confidence filters.

• August to October 2026 uses early data that may change.

• The full list is on the website.

TOOLS

Python, pandas, numpy, matplotlib, Google Colab, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, GitHub Pages.
